metadata.title: Claude, Deal Sourcing.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: what does the word 'skill' actually add to Claude when you install deal-sourcing? Take the file apart and show the mechanism — a folder holding one SKILL.md, three ordered steps — then name the design choice: guaranteed checklist execution at the expense of any investment judgment about the results.

beats.narration_text: Read 'Claude has a deal-sourcing skill' and it sounds like Claude decides which companies to invest in. It doesn't — it just finds candidates. Let's open that file and see how it actually works.

beats.narration_text: Here's where the framing does the damage. The word 'skill' is carrying a lot of freight — it sounds like Claude picked up investment judgment, like it can look at a company and tell you whether it's worth backing. That's the natural read; it's also the wrong one.

Nothing in the model changes. Delete the folder and no judgment leaves the building — there was none in there to lose. The weights are the same before and after; what you lose is the three-step routine Claude was reading off the page. The checklist is gone; the taste never existed.

Here's what a skill actually is: one file. A folder called deal-sourcing, and inside it a single SKILL.md — three steps, written out, in order. One: search a sector for target companies. Two: check the CRM for existing relationships. Three: draft a personalized outreach email to the founder. That's the whole file — an ordered checklist, in plain English.

Claude reads the file top to bottom and walks the steps as written: search the sector, check the CRM, draft the email. No branching, no shortcuts — unless the file itself says branch. The design choice worth naming: put the routine in a document, not in the weights. It's the same routine every run because it's the same document every run.

That makes a skill a specification, not new judgment. They optimized for guaranteed consistency at the expense of guaranteed judgment. The payoff: the same three steps, every sector, every time — no drift. The limit: ranking those candidates by how good an investment they'd be — that isn't on the page, so Claude doesn't do it.

So deal-sourcing never handed Claude judgment about which deals are good. What it guarantees is much narrower: every run, Claude opens the same file and walks the same three steps. That's the whole trick. The mechanism is the checklist; the mechanism is not the taste that would rank the results.

beats.narration_text: Watch Claude surface twenty candidate companies and you've proven the search step ran. You haven't proven any of the twenty are worth backing — that judgment is somewhere else. Watch it draft a clean, personalized outreach email and you've proven the drafting step ran. You haven't proven the founder will ever reply. Ran-the-step and worked are two different claims.
A skill named deal-sourcing doesn't hand Claude investment judgment — it finds candidate companies and drafts the outreach; whether any of it's a good deal is still on you.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Pick one repeatable search-and-outreach routine you already run — sourcing candidates for anything, not just deals — and ask the model to write you a SKILL.md for it: three to five steps, in order, plain English, each one specific enough that a stranger could execute it the same way every time. Then have it read the file back and walk through exactly what it'll do before it does it. Go deeper: after the walk-through, ask which step in your routine actually requires judgment that isn't written on the page — that's the seam between the checklist and you.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want a SKILL.md for a repeatable search-and-outreach routine I already run — for example, sourcing candidates for [pick one: podcast guests, freelance clients, hires, deals, speakers, sponsors]. Write it as a folder-plus-single-file skill: three to five steps in order, in plain English, each one specific enough that a stranger could execute it the same way every time. Say what to search, what to check, and what to produce at the end. Then read the file back to me and walk through exactly what you'll do, in order, before you do it.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: after the walk-through, ask which step in the routine actually requires judgment that isn't written on the page — that's the seam between what a checklist can do and what you still have to do.
